lines.text: Chapter two, section one. Overview and objectives.
In the first chapter we used a purely polarized toy game to isolate leverage, but real hands rarely split cleanly into pure value and pure air.
Most bets you actually make on the flop and turn get value from two very different places at the same time.
One source is fold equity, which is money you win when your opponent gives up and folds.
The other is pot equity, which is your share of the pot if the hand goes to showdown right now, before any more chips move.
A bluff is a hand that gets most of its value from fold equity, and a value bet is a hand that gets most of its value from pot equity, but the line between them is fuzzy well before the river.
This chapter is about the hands that live in the middle: hands that would rather not go to showdown against a strong range, but still have enough equity to be worth playing aggressively.
By the end of the chapter you should be able to explain when a medium-strength hand should bet for protection instead of check-calling.
You should be able to recognize when a range should be linear, meaning it excludes the weakest hands, rather than fully polarized.
You should be able to spot the situations where a modest equity advantage makes small-bet strategies extremely profitable.
And you should be able to resist the human urge to over-complicate a strategy that only barely improves on a much simpler one.
